The sensitivity of current gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by sensor noise, creating a "noise floor" that limits their ability to identify gravitational wave signals. Specifically, the high-frequency sensitivity of interferometric sensors is limited by shot noise, which depends on the light power within the instrument. Using a non-standard data analysis approach, we evaluate the sloshing-Sagnac's sensitivity and spectral density, comparing its performance against current and future generations of interferometric sensors, including stacked designs like the APEX. This study examines basic global atmospheric circulation patterns in simplified one- and two-layer shallow water models on a rotating sphere, considering both uniform and differential rotation. Using comparative fluid dynamics, the authors identify distinct circulation regimes based on the planetary vorticity ($\Omega$), equatorial beta parameter ($\beta$), and initial relative vorticity ($\zeta_0$). In the absence of friction, these regimes range from solid-body rotation to turbulent flow, with transitional patterns involving vortex generation and wave activity. When friction is introduced, vortex formation leads to westward drift, ultimately resulting in a statistically steady state characterized by westward waves and eddies. Notably, this final state exhibits turbulent characteristics, with turbulence intensity increasing as drag coefficients decrease. These findings offer insights into atmospheric dynamics on Earth, Mars, and Titan, as well as the gas disks surrounding young stars. We introduce a stochastic hydrodynamic framework designed to examine the thermal fluctuations of interacting quantum Bose fluids within the phase-space. This approach, termed rQHD-$\phi$, integrates the quantum Keldysh formalism, the phase-space representation of quantum fields, and a rationalized random hydrodynamic model. By employing a simple 1D interacting quantum Bose model as a test case, we compare field-theoretic and many-body calculations of correlations in both momentum and position domains against established results from kinetic theory, many-body theory, and molecular dynamics simulations. The validity of the rQHD-$\phi$ is confirmed through these simulations, highlighting its potential to serve as an effective tool for investigating quantum fluctuations in the space of quantum phases. Specifically, this model offers a rationalized alternative for analyzing real-time dynamics in quantum Bose models, potentially facilitating the exploration of non-equilibrium phenomena, such as post-quench evolution, without relying on specific model dependencies. Complementing this, we develop a linearized version of the rQHD-$\phi$, known as lrQHD-$\phi$, to serve as a practical tool for predicting real-time dynamics in complex interacting quantum Bose systems. Finally, we report initial findings derived from this linearized approach regarding the post-quench dynamics of a 1D Bose gas following sudden changes in interaction strength. These experiments demonstrate that the lrQHD-$\phi$ accurately predicts the characteristic non-equilibrium hydrodynamic modes observed in molecular dynamics simulations when the interaction is turned on suddenly. Furthermore, when the interaction is switched off suddenly, the model correctly anticipates the emergence of massless hydrodynamic modes, manifesting as sound waves. These results underscore the value of the rQHD family of models as a rationalized framework for exploring non-equilibrium phenomena in interacting quantum Bose systems. An Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent capable of learning new tasks from human guidance, such as providing answers to queries, is known as an Learning AI (LAI). The frameworks guiding this learning process are termed Education Frameworks (EdF), which, although widely discussed in academic literature, lack a unified definition and taxonomy. Similarly, Knowledge Acquisition (KA)—the method by which an LAI obtains information—remains poorly understood and systematically examined. This paper defines and examines Knowledge Acquisition, offering a comprehensive survey that characterizes its goals, strategies, evaluation metrics, and underlying technical methods. We introduce a systematic taxonomy for EdFs and classify various KA methods within this structure, concurrently defining a corresponding taxonomy for KA itself. We further analyze the relationships between EdF frameworks and specific KA methods, as well as different methods among themselves. Accompanying these discussions, we summarize related concepts, including Taxonomy Learning, Few-Shot Learning, and Large Language Models. Finally, we explore future research directions for both EdFs and KAs. To support this survey, we develop an open-source platform called "WikiEducator," a collaborative portal designed to define, categorize, and examine Education and Knowledge Acquisition frameworks alongside their associated methods (illustrated in Figure 1). This platform will serve as a resource for understanding and developing EdFs, KAs, and their respective methodologies. The surveys presented in this paper and at the co-organized workshops during DAC'23 are collected in the special issue of IEEE CDATA[1]. We hope this work aids in systematizing Research Frameworks (RF) and associated methods across diverse domains, potentially benefiting other fields as well. The Message Passing Algorithm (MPA) is a powerful technique widely employed in decoding codes, performing inference, and optimizing structural graphical models, including trees, acyclic graphs, and those with near-cyclic structures. While numerous variants of MPA have been proposed, they often lack practical implementation due to complexity or insufficient accuracy. This study introduces an updated iterative algorithm termed "Tight-PEMPA," which offers a unified framework delivering more accurate inference and optimization for graphical models without sacrificing computational efficiency. Specifically, this work presents a concise description of PEMP (Partial Exact Message Passing), a refined version of MPA, and demonstrates its application in optimizing both undirected Markov Random Fields (MRF) and their directed counterparts, Directed Acyclic Models (DAM). The proposed framework delivers a state-of-the-art constrained optimization algorithm for DAMs. Experimental results on small-scale graphical models confirm that this approach outperforms existing methods, such as Mean Field, MPL, and MPW. These findings indicate that this constraint-based optimization algorithm is significantly more accurate than previous iterative algorithms, including Mean Variance Loss (MVL) and L-BFGS-based solutions. Building on these findings, they investigate whether simple bulge fraction models can account for the overall shape of the $\M*-SFR$ curve, particularly at the turnover point. They establish a method to estimate the turnover mass as a function of bulge fraction and brine, predicting a lowest possible turnover mass of approximately $10^{10.9}\Sun$ for the most central galaxies. Finally, they discuss how this model aligns with observed trends in specific bulge indicators against stellar mass and the specific SFR ($sSFR$) alongside the $\M*-SFR$ relation, while also highlighting remaining challenges. The study emphasizes that future observations require more direct probes of bulge presence or formation mechanisms at high redshift to better constrain this model. Additionally, they advocate for incorporating bulge fraction trends into cosmological simulations to elucidate the physical basis of the baryon-to-stellar mass efficiency's turnover and the resulting turnoff in the $\M*-SFR$ curve at high masses. This work represents a follow-up to the study: What turns on and then off starformation in massive galaxies? The influence of the baryon-to-stellar mass efficiency ($\eta_*$).

Although existing identification methods rely heavily on model-specific features from both real and labeled fake articles, these approaches struggle to generalize to new models and remain ineffective when sufficient labeled examples are unavailable. Segmental evaluation in medical imaging is frequently compromised by noise introduced through manual annotation. To mitigate this, Cerebral Lesion Generation (CLG) serves as a pre-training strategy designed to produce refined lesion masks automatically. This paper introduces a new framework for CLG that integrates an domain generator and a domain discriminator into a progressive training structure. Initially, the domain generator enhances the realism of synthetic lesion masks. Subsequently, the domain discriminator offers unsupervised feedback to further polish these masks before they enter the segmentation module. Evaluated on two standard datasets, MICCAIlesion CT and MICCAIlesion MR, the proposed method achieves an overall Segmentation Accuracy of 84.04% on the MICCAIlesion CT dataset and 80.12% on the MICCAIlesion MR dataset. The approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through quantitative metrics that indicate higher consistency between generated and actual lesion masks, as well as lower label noise. Visual comparisons and per-class accuracy metrics confirm the efficacy of CLG in reducing annotation noise. Implementing this method requires only the existing training pipeline; no additional annotation efforts are necessary. Consequently, CLG presents a practical solution for refining manually segmented lesions in protocols like MICCAIlesion CT/MR and has been adopted by the 2020 MICCAI Lesion Segmentation working track. Large language models (LLMs) integrate knowledge from textual sources, such as articles and encyclopedias, with structured data like databases and knowledge graphs. This paper examines how LLMs retrieve information from these structured formats, a process beginning with generating SQL queries for relational databases or performing graph traversals for knowledge graphs. We provide a comprehensive review of existing methods for these initial generation steps across both database and knowledge graph systems. Furthermore, we identify gaps in current approaches and propose a framework capable of accessing, Traversing, and integrating knowledge from various structured repositories without requiring pre-trained modules for specific systems. We define this framework as ability-knowledge integration (AI), positioning it as a foundational capability for LLMs to utilize multiple knowledge sources, whether they are traditional structured data, unstructured text, or emerging formats like tabular or video data. To illustrate AI in action, we introduce MetaPentup, a framework that fuses a corporate database with five distinct knowledge graphs to support advanced business intelligence tasks. Our demonstrations confirm that knowledge graphs can offer more granular details than databases for certain queries, while the MetaPentup system effectively combines both sources to deliver comprehensive answers. Additionally, we present comprehensive benchmarks for these demonstrations and introduce a suite of multi-source benchmarks designed to evaluate the AI capabilities of state-of-the-art LLM-based systems. To facilitate this assessment, we developed an automated testing framework that generates and executes SQL queries and knowledge graph traversal sequences across our database and graph sources to align with task specifications. We utilize these benchmarks to compare our framework against existing LLM solutions, highlighting the specialized advantages of MetaPentup in this domain. The framework's code and datasets are accessible at https://github.com/ucsc-vllm/MetaPentup. Ultimately, this work provides a thorough analysis of how LLMs incorporate knowledge from structured repositories, introduces a universal framework for integrating multiple knowledge sources, and establishes benchmarks to measure this capability across the community. Our results demonstrate that MetaPentup effectively combines textual, relational, and graph-based knowledge to address complex reasoning challenges, outperforming other state-of-the-art systems by approximately 20% on our proposed benchmarks. Our framework serves as a versatile platform for evaluating LLMs against multiple knowledge sources, applicable to foundational models, chatbots, and reasoning-based tasks. Non-linear charged Anti-de Sitter (AdS) black holes, whose field equations admit two distinct black hole horizons for specific parameter ranges, are examined within the framework of geometric thermodynamics. This study focuses on non-linear electrodynamics (NLE) modeled as the sum of two rational functions, a model proposed by Hoyle and Olum. Utilizing the shadow radius as an intensive parameter, we define a new legitimacy phase transition based on the shadow radius–entropy ($r_s$--$S$) graph. The results indicate that for non-linear charge parameters $\gamma<0.4334$, the $r_s$--$S$ curve exhibits an "S"-shaped trajectory, signaling the existence of a shadow legitimacy phase transition analogous to a second-order thermodynamic phase transition. When $\gamma$ exceeds this critical value, the curve becomes monotonic, and the legitimacy phase transition disappears. Furthermore, for fixed shadow radius and non-linear charge, both the entropy and legitimacy density display a step-like variation as the non-linear parameter $\beta$ increases. Finally, thermal density graphs reveal that the specific heat capacity per shadow radius diverges at the critical shadow radius corresponding to the critical non-linear charge, highlighting the significant impact of non-linearity on this capacity. The intricate relationship between the shadow radius, charge, and non-linearity parameter alongside the specific heat capacity per shadow radius underscores the utility of the shadow radius as a fundamental variable in black hole thermodynamics. These findings suggest that the shadow radius can serve as an effective order parameter in investigating black hole thermodynamic behaviors, particularly when traditional temperature and specific heat capacity per unit volume are difficult to measure. Additionally, this work establishes a direct link between the black hole shadow and its specific heat capacity, offering fresh insights into the physical significance of the shadow. Our analysis suggests that the non-linear charge parameter $\gamma$ functions as a "shadow quality" parameter, influencing the shadow's size and confirming the utility of the shadow radius as an intensive variable in non-linear charged AdS black hole thermodynamics. The underlying thermodynamic characteristics of this system are illustrated through various graphical representations.

Furthermore, the notion of deformation in tomograms can be extended to other representations, potentially serving as a universal metric for quantumness across different frameworks. We investigate the acoustic emissions generated by an adhesive tape as it is unwound from a roll and crossed over itself before being unwound again to straighten it. Using wavelet analysis to examine the signal spectrum and visualizing the corresponding acoustic waveform, we identify distinct stages in the noise evolution that align with-tentatively-specific peeling mechanisms. These stages exhibit clear fractal characteristics, as evidenced by burst-like noise and a straight line in the Hurst exponent versus scale plot. Furthermore, a Fractal Fuzzy Bursts model effectively captures this fractal fractious bursty noise pattern. Notably, both the Hurst exponent and the dominant frequency of the bursts display abrupt changes at precise moments, indicating underlying ordered structural shifts; this is particularly apparent in the Hurst exponent when plotted against time. The presence of this concealed order during the transition between different bursting noises supports the hypothesis that the system becomes trapped in a metastable state prior to suddenly switching mechanisms. These findings provide a foundation for exploring noise-induced transitions in other systems. Additionally, the initial fractal characteristics of the acoustic emissions during the tape's unrolling confirm a multi-fractal nature, mirroring the multi-fractal crackling noise observed in various materials under stress. This confirms that "fractality" originates from step-by-step fractal-like behaviors linked to shifting mechanisms, a concept potentially applicable across diverse materials exhibiting crackling sound under stress. We conclude by outlining the sequential mechanisms responsible for the observed acoustic emissions during the tape's unrolling. These mechanisms include: (i) sudden snapping of polymer chains at the tip of the already peeled section, (ii) sticking and subsequent snapping of the tape's backside against the roller, and (iii) gradual transitions in how the adhesive tape peels. These mechanisms may also account for the multi-fractal crackling noise seen when other adhesive tapes or materials are stretched. These structures are typically derived from raw point clouds via smoothing techniques essential for anomaly detection methods like Deep Set Convolutional Networks and Network Embedding-based approaches. However, existing methods often introduce biases that compromise detection efficacy or demand substantial computational resources. This paper presents the Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC) method, which generates a strictly unique, bias-free, and efficient representation of raw point clouds.
